title: OpenAI to Add Invisible Text Watermarks to ChatGPT and Codex in the EU
excerpt: OpenAI's textGrain system subtly shapes word choices so detectors can spot AI-generated text, complying with the EU AI Act. API developers worldwide can opt in; the detector stays limited to approved researchers.
body:
• OpenAI announced on October 5 that it will add an invisible statistical watermark, called textGrain, to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text generated in the European Union over the coming weeks, across all plans — complying with the EU AI Act's transparency rules in effect since August 2.
  • Developers using OpenAI's API anywhere in the world can opt in to watermarking for select models starting today; it is off by default and OpenAI said it will not become a global default at launch. The option arrives on Microsoft Azure in the coming weeks.
  • The watermark is invisible and travels with text when copied and pasted, but it is fragile: OpenAI's tests show replacing just 10% of words with synonyms drops detection from about 92% to 66%. Short passages, math answers and translated text are harder to detect.
  • For users: the watermark does not identify you, and OpenAI saw no meaningful performance change with it on. The detector goes only to approved researchers and expert organizations initially — no public "ChatGPT detector" ships with this, and a missing watermark "does not prove human authorship."

OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union, the company said Monday in a blog post, making it the latest AI lab to mark machine-generated text under the EU AI Act. The watermark rolls out over the coming weeks to eligible users across all plans in the EU. Developers using OpenAI's API anywhere in the world can switch it on for select models starting today — though it is off by default, and OpenAI said it will not become a global default at launch.

The EU AI Act's transparency rules, in effect since August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI have all committed to the EU's code of practice on AI-generated content.

Context and Background

OpenAI had built text watermarking years ago but kept it on the shelf. In 2024, the Wall Street Journal reported the company held back partly over fears users would defect to rivals that didn't watermark. Regulation changed the calculus: OpenAI signed the EU's code of practice for general-purpose AI in July 2025, and from August 2, 2026 the AI Act's transparency article applied to text. Google runs a text watermark in Gemini and Anthropic ships one in Claude — ChatGPT was the last big holdout.

Anthropic's decision two months ago to watermark Claude's text globally drew backlash from users who argued they had supplied "the instructions, context, decisions" while Claude was merely "the tool." OpenAI is taking the narrower route: EU-only for consumer products, opt-in everywhere for the API.

Impact and Analysis

The watermark is not a visible symbol or hidden character. It works by subtly shaping the model's word choices during generation — a statistical pattern readers can't see but a detector can pick up. OpenAI published a technical report on the method, called textGrain, co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, describing how a secret key sorts next-word predictions as each sentence forms. Because the signal lives in the words themselves, it survives copy-and-paste and travels with the text.

"Watermarks can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it."

— OpenAI

OpenAI is unusually candid about the limitations. Editing weakens the watermark: replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. Short passages, math answers and translated text are harder to detect. A missing watermark "does not prove human authorship," the company cautioned — the text could be too short, too heavily edited, or generated by another company's AI.

Those limits drove the access decision: the detector will initially be available only to approved researchers and expert organizations. OpenAI's framing is pointed — textGrain is a provenance signal, not an AI detector that proves who wrote a document. A positive result can indicate OpenAI tooling likely generated or processed some of the text; a negative result proves nothing.

Diaspora Angle

Users outside the EU are unaffected for now — watermarking is EU-only for consumers and opt-in on the API. But educators, employers and compliance teams should note the direction of travel: machine-readable marking of AI-generated text is now law in one major jurisdiction, and these watermarks are invisible, fragile and — outside the EU — often absent entirely.

What's Next

Watch the EU rollout for user pushback like Anthropic's, whether detector access broadens beyond approved researchers, and whether regulators accept textGrain as sufficient compliance. The longer-term question is whether other jurisdictions follow with their own transparency rules, which would force OpenAI to revisit its no-global-default stance.
